summary.text:
A district council with a large housing account and a treasury position that is small on the investment side and substantial on the debt side. At 30 June 2026 it held £9.5m of investments against £118.1m of external borrowing — so this is a borrower, and what happens to borrowing rates matters to it far more than what happens to deposit rates.

The debt is all fixed rate and mostly long: 71% of it matures in ten years or more, and the average rate across the book is 3.65%. £93.8m of it is PWLB across 32 separate loans at an average of 3.52%, with £10m from Barclays at 4.24% and £10m borrowed from two other councils at 4.05% and 4.60%. That average rate is the important number, because it was struck in a different rate environment from the one the council would borrow in today.

The council is £42.0m under-borrowed against a capital financing requirement of £160.4m — it has spent the money and not yet raised the debt, funding the gap from its own cash. That is a deliberate and common choice, and it saves money while it lasts. It also means the council has £42m of borrowing still to do, at whatever rates apply when it does it.

Two ratios stand out. Financing costs take 30.64% of the HRA's net revenue stream — close to a third of housing income going on debt service, and the council expects to borrow more for the HRA. On the General Fund the figure is 15.18%. Separately, 14.05% of the General Fund's net revenue stream comes from commercial and service investments, which is a real dependence on income that is not council tax or grant.

Nothing here is a breach. Officers confirm the approved limits were not exceeded during the quarter, and the investment side is run conservatively — 100% in specified investments against a 25% minimum, all of it in two money market funds available on call, yielding 3.98% against a SONIA average of 3.73%. The questions worth asking are about the direction of travel, not about compliance.

7523.summary:
Executive is asked to note the Q1 treasury and prudential position. It is a noting item, which in practice is the only routine opportunity members get to question treasury decisions before they are made.

Two things in the paper deserve a question. The first is capital: the General Fund capital programme has gone from an original estimate of £6.574m approved in March to a revised £25.944m at Q1 — close to four times the budget, in one quarter. The paper says this reflects schemes "approved by or subject to approval since" the March budget, but does not list them. The second is the interest rate forecast the report relies on, which is dated 25 March 2026 and is being put to a meeting on 18 August.

questions.q: The General Fund capital programme has gone from £6.574m at the March budget to £25.944m at Q1. What are the schemes behind the £19.4m increase, and which of them has this Executive actually approved?
questions.why: Appendix A gives the movement but not the causes. A near-fourfold increase inside one quarter either reflects grant-funded schemes that carry no borrowing — in which case it is good news and should be said — or it adds to the £42m of borrowing still to be raised.

questions.q: The rate forecast this report relies on is dated 25 March. Since then the 10-year gilt has traded between 4.69% and 5.18%. What would the £42.0m of under-borrowing cost at today's PWLB rates rather than at the 3.52% average we currently pay?
questions.why: The council's existing PWLB book averages 3.52%. New long-dated PWLB borrowing today costs materially more than that. The gap between the two is the single largest financial risk in this report, and the report does not quantify it.

questions.q: Financing costs already take 30.64% of the HRA's net revenue stream, and paragraph 4.3.4 says further HRA borrowing is anticipated. At what ratio does the council consider the HRA to be at its limit?
questions.why: There is no statutory cap, which is exactly why the council needs its own answer. Nearly a third of housing revenue is already committed to debt service before any new borrowing.

questions.q: 14.05% of the net revenue stream comes from commercial and service investments. What is the current valuation of those assets against what was paid, and what happens to the budget if that income falls?
questions.why: The indicator is reported as a percentage without the underlying assets or their values. Councils elsewhere have found commercial income harder to sustain than expected.

questions.q: All £9.5m of investments sit in two money market funds. What is the maximum exposure the strategy allows to a single fund, and how close are we to it?
questions.why: £7.0m of the £9.5m is in one fund. The security and liquidity positions are genuinely strong — this is about concentration, not credit quality, and the answer may well be reassuring.

email.subject: Your Executive meeting on 18 August — five questions on the treasury report
email.body:
Dear Councillor,

Your Executive meets on Tuesday 18 August with a treasury management and prudential code update on the agenda. We track council treasury papers and PWLB borrowing rates, and we have read this one. It is a well-put-together report and the council's own performance in it is good, so this note is not a criticism — it is the set of questions we would want answered if we were sitting in the meeting.

What the report shows, briefly. The council held £9.5m of investments at 30 June, all of it in low-risk specified investments against a 25% minimum, earning 3.98% while the SONIA benchmark averaged 3.73%. Officers confirm no approved limit was breached. On the investment side this is a tidy position, run properly.

The borrowing side is where the money is. The council owes £118.1m, all fixed rate, at an average of 3.65%. It is also £42.0m under-borrowed against its capital financing requirement — money already spent on capital that has not yet been raised as debt, funded meanwhile from the council's own cash.

Five questions we would ask:

1. The General Fund capital programme has gone from £6.574m in the March budget to £25.944m at Q1 — nearly four times, in one quarter. Which schemes, and which of them has the Executive approved?

2. The interest rate forecast in the report is dated 25 March. What would the £42.0m of under-borrowing cost at today's PWLB rates, rather than at the 3.52% the existing PWLB book averages?

3. Financing costs already take 30.64% of the HRA's net revenue stream, and the report says further HRA borrowing is anticipated. At what ratio does the council consider that too high?

4. 14.05% of net revenue comes from commercial and service investments. What are those assets worth today against what was paid for them?

5. All £9.5m of investments sits in two money market funds, £7.0m of it in one. What is the concentration limit?

Question 2 is the one we would press. The council's existing debt was borrowed in a cheaper era. The £42m still to be raised will not be, and the report does not put a number on that difference.

Every figure above is from the Executive's own paper, and we are happy to send the page references.

If it is useful, PWLBtoday runs short courses for councillors on reading treasury reports and on what the prudential indicators actually mean. They are written for members rather than accountants. Details are at pwlbtoday.org, and there is no charge for asking us a question either way.

With best wishes,

PWLBtoday
